auxiliary_material.content: Preclinical models (Vétizou et al., Routy et al., Sivan et al.) demonstrate that commensal bacteria influence antigen presentation, dendritic cell maturation, and CD8+ T-cell priming. Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis disrupts these processes, leading to impaired immune surveillance. FMT from responders can restore sensitivity to PD-1 blockade in refractory patients (Davar et al., Kim et al.).

Evidence consistently suggests that the detrimental association is most pronounced when antibiotics are administered shortly before ICI initiation (pre-treatment window). Concurrent or post-treatment exposure shows more variable or null effects in several studies (e.g., Pinato 2019, Chorti 2024).

Most retrospective studies did not detect statistically significant differences between antibiotic categories (beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones). It is unclear if specific classes drive the effect or if broad-spectrum activity/spectrum of activity is the critical determinant. Few studies accounted for infection severity or indication.

Judicious antibiotic stewardship is recommended, particularly avoiding unnecessary/prolonged exposure in the peri-immunotherapy period. However, antibiotics should not be withheld when clinically indicated due to severe infection risk.

outline_action: Use the provided material to construct the section on 'Clinical Evidence of Antibiotic Impact on ICI Outcomes'. Structure by timing (prior vs. concurrent) and tumor type (Melanoma, NSCLC, RCC, HCC). Highlight the consistent signal of reduced PFS/OS with pre-treatment exposure. Explicitly note the limitations regarding confounding by indication and the lack of causal proof despite biological plausibility. Include the neutral finding from Kaderbhai to illustrate heterogeneity. Use the auxiliary mechanism material to support the biological rationale for the observed associations.
remaining_gap: ['The gap question asks how adjustment for clinical confounding affects interpretation. While this review provides adjusted results for several key studies (e.g., Pinato 2019, Derosa 2018), it explicitly states that causality cannot be definitively established due to confounding by indication (infection severity, baseline fitness) which may not be fully captured in multivariate models. The review does not provide a comprehensive synthesis of *how* different adjustment strategies across all available literature alter the magnitude of the effect size compared to unadjusted estimates, nor does it resolve the extent of residual confounding.', 'The specific contribution of antibiotic *class* or *spectrum* remains unresolved, as the review notes insufficient power and reporting in existing studies to determine class-specific effects.']
